lessonTitle: Acute Kidney Injury and Chronic Kidney Disease: Classification and Consequences

blocks.text: A 71-year-old man has had three days of vomiting and diarrhoea. He kept taking his usual ramipril and, for aching muscles, ibuprofen. Today he has passed almost no urine, and his creatinine has doubled from its baseline. His kidneys, starved of perfusion and denied their normal compensating prostaglandins, have stopped filtering. Whether this recovers depends on recognising where the problem lies.

blocks.title: Acute kidney injury
blocks.text: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an abrupt decline in kidney function over hours to days. A common consensus definition is a rise in serum creatinine of at least 26.5 micromol/L (0.3 mg/dL) within 48 hours, a rise to at least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Thresholds are set by guideline and vary slightly between them.

blocks.markdown: The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of plasma filtered per minute and is the best overall index of kidney function. Creatinine is freely filtered and little secreted, so its **clearance** approximates GFR. Clinically, GFR is usually estimated (eGFR) from serum creatinine, age and sex.

blocks.caption: Creatinine clearance (mL/min). U = urine creatinine concentration, V = urine flow rate (mL/min), P = plasma creatinine concentration; U and P use the same units.

blocks.title: Creatinine clearance from a 24-hour collection
blocks.prompt: A patient has urine creatinine 6000 micromol/L, a 24-hour urine volume of 1.44 L, and plasma creatinine 120 micromol/L. Calculate the creatinine clearance.

steps.text: Convert volume to a flow rate: 1.44 L = 1440 mL per 1440 minutes = 1.0 mL/min.
Apply the formula: clearance = 6000 x 1.0 / 120 = 50 mL/min.
Compare with the staging bands: 45-59 mL/min corresponds to G3a, mildly to moderately reduced.

blocks.answer: Creatinine clearance is 50 mL/min, which falls in the G3a band.

blocks.markdown:
### Classification of AKI: prerenal, intrinsic, postrenal

AKI is classified by **where the problem lies relative to the kidney**. **Prerenal** AKI is reduced renal perfusion with structurally normal kidneys, which recovers if perfusion is restored. **Intrinsic (renal)** AKI is damage to the nephron itself: the tubules (acute tubular necrosis, ATN), glomeruli (glomerulonephritis), interstitium (acute interstitial nephritis) or renal vessels. **Postrenal** AKI is obstruction to urine flow, from the renal pelvis down to the urethra, and requires bilateral obstruction (or obstruction of a single functioning kidney) to produce a rise in creatinine.

rows: Reduced renal blood flow; functional response
Hypovolaemia, haemorrhage, heart failure, sepsis, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors in a volume-depleted patient
Urine concentrated, low urinary sodium, raised urea to creatinine ratio; responds to fluids
Tubular, glomerular, interstitial or vascular injury
ATN (ischaemia, toxins, aminoglycosides, contrast), glomerulonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis
Muddy brown granular casts in ATN; isosthenuria; urinary sodium high
Prostatic enlargement, bladder or pelvic tumour, bilateral stones, retroperitoneal fibrosis
Anuria or fluctuating urine volume, hydronephrosis on ultrasound
blocks.caption: AKI classified by site

blocks.title: Separating prerenal AKI from ATN
blocks.prompt: Two patients have AKI. Patient A has urine sodium 12 mmol/L and urine osmolality 640 mOsm/kg. Patient B has urine sodium 55 mmol/L and urine osmolality 310 mOsm/kg. Which has prerenal AKI and which ATN?

steps.text: In prerenal AKI the tubules are healthy, so they respond to low perfusion by avidly reabsorbing sodium and water. This gives low urine sodium (commonly below about 20 mmol/L) and concentrated urine (osmolality above about 500 mOsm/kg).
In ATN the tubular cells are damaged and cannot reabsorb sodium or concentrate the filtrate. Urine sodium is high (commonly above about 40 mmol/L) and urine is close to plasma osmolality (about 300).
Patient A fits the first pattern; Patient B fits the second. These cut-offs are guides and vary between sources.

blocks.answer: Patient A has prerenal AKI and Patient B has acute tubular necrosis.

blocks.markdown:
### Chronic kidney disease and its staging

**Chronic kidney disease (CKD)** is abnormal kidney structure or function present for more than 3 months with implications for health. It is staged on two axes because both predict outcome. GFR categories G1 to G5 describe filtering capacity, and albuminuria categories A1 to A3, based on the urine albumin to creatinine ratio (ACR), describe glomerular leak. Albuminuria matters because it signals glomerular damage and is an independent predictor of progression and cardiovascular events.

blocks.caption: CKD categories by eGFR and albuminuria (G1-G2 count as CKD only with other evidence of kidney damage)

blocks.markdown:
### Metabolic complications of advanced renal failure

As nephrons are lost, the failing kidney can no longer perform its excretory, regulatory and endocrine functions. Consequences include **hyperkalaemia** (reduced potassium excretion), **metabolic acidosis** (reduced hydrogen ion excretion and ammonia generation), **anaemia** (reduced erythropoietin from peritubular interstitial cells), **fluid overload and hypertension** (sodium and water retention), and **uraemia**, the retention of urea and other toxins causing nausea, pruritus, pericarditis and encephalopathy. Disordered mineral metabolism, **CKD-mineral and bone disorder**, follows reduced phosphate excretion (**hyperphosphataemia**) and reduced activation of vitamin D by renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, giving low calcitriol, **hypocalcaemia** and **secondary hyperparathyroidism**.

items: Hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis from impaired tubular excretion.
Hyperphosphataemia, low calcitriol, hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism leading to renal bone disease.
Salt and water retention, hypertension and pulmonary oedema.
Uraemic symptoms: nausea, pruritus, pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding tendency.

blocks.title: AKI and CKD are linked
blocks.text: AKI is potentially reversible if the cause is corrected early, but severe or repeated episodes can leave residual loss of nephrons and predispose to CKD. Diabetes and hypertension are the leading causes of CKD, and CKD in turn increases susceptibility to AKI.

points: AKI is classified as prerenal (low perfusion), intrinsic (tubular, glomerular, interstitial or vascular damage) or postrenal (obstruction), and the urine findings help separate prerenal disease from ATN.
CKD is staged by eGFR (G1-G5) and albuminuria (A1-A3), present for more than 3 months, and both axes predict outcome.
Advanced renal failure causes hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, anaemia, hyperphosphataemia with hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism, fluid overload and uraemia.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with prostatic enlargement has a creatinine that has doubled over three days. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis. How is this AKI classified?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: obstruction to urine outflow causing hydronephrosis is postrenal AKI.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: prerenal AKI results from reduced renal perfusion and does not cause hydronephrosis.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: tubular necrosis would not cause bilateral hydronephrosis.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: glomerular disease is not associated with dilated collecting systems.

questions.explanation: Bilateral hydronephrosis in a man with prostatic enlargement indicates obstruction at or below the bladder outlet. Relief of the obstruction, for example by catheterisation, can restore function.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man in septic shock has been hypotensive for 12 hours. His urine output has fallen to almost nothing despite fluids, and urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts. What is the likely cause of his AKI?

options.text: Simple prerenal hypoperfusion that will correct with fluid alone
Acute interstitial nephritis from drug hypersensitivity

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prolonged ischaemia kills tubular epithelium, which sloughs and forms muddy brown casts.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: prerenal AKI has a bland sediment and responds quickly to restoring perfusion.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: interstitial nephritis typically shows white cell casts and eosinophils.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: obstruction would not produce granular casts.

questions.explanation: Sustained hypotension causes ischaemic injury of the tubular epithelium, called acute tubular necrosis. Muddy brown granular casts are the characteristic urinary finding, and failure to respond to fluids suggests established tubular damage.

questions.stem: A patient has an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m^2 and a urine ACR of 45 mg/mmol, both persisting over 4 months. What is the CKD category?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: eGFR 30-44 is G3b, and ACR above 30 mg/mmol is A3.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: G3a is 45-59 and A2 is ACR 3-30.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: G4 is 15-29 and A1 is below 3.

questions.explanation: The eGFR of 38 lies between 30 and 44, which is G3b, and an ACR of 45 mg/mmol exceeds 30, which is A3. Abnormalities must persist for more than 3 months to define CKD.

questions.stem: Which mechanism is mainly responsible for anaemia in advanced chronic kidney disease?

options.text: Reduced erythropoietin production by the failing kidney
Intravascular haemolysis from uraemic toxins as the primary cause

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced erythropoietin production by the failing kidney

distractorRationale.a: Correct: peritubular interstitial cells make erythropoietin and are lost in CKD.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: erythropoietin is deficient, not in excess.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: B12 malabsorption is not a feature of CKD.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: uraemia may shorten red cell survival slightly but is not the main cause.

questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is produced by interstitial cells in the renal cortex in response to hypoxia. As nephrons are lost, erythropoietin falls and the marrow makes too few red cells, giving a normocytic normochromic anaemia.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m^2 has a low serum calcium, a high serum phosphate and a raised parathyroid hormone. Which is the best explanation?

options.text: Phosphate retention and reduced calcitriol synthesis driving secondary hyperparathyroidism
A parathyroid adenoma causing primary hyperparathyroidism

questions.correctOptionText: Phosphate retention and reduced calcitriol synthesis driving secondary hyperparathyroidism

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the failing kidney retains phosphate and cannot make calcitriol, so calcium falls and PTH rises.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: primary hyperparathyroidism would give a high calcium.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: excess calcium would not give hypocalcaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: vitamin D toxicity raises calcium.

questions.explanation: Reduced phosphate excretion and reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity lower calcium, which stimulates the parathyroids. This is secondary hyperparathyroidism, a component of CKD-mineral and bone disorder.

questions.stem: A 24-hour urine collection from a patient has a volume of 1.8 L and a urine creatinine concentration of 4500 micromol/L. Plasma creatinine is 150 micromol/L. Calculate creatinine clearance in mL/min.
questions.explanation: Urine flow is 1800 mL per 1440 min = 1.25 mL/min. Clearance = U x V / P = 4500 x 1.25 / 150 = 37.5 mL/min, which lies in the G3b band.

questions.stem: An 80 kg patient on intensive care is being monitored for AKI. Using the criterion of urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours, what total urine volume over the 6 hours falls below the threshold? Give the threshold volume in mL.
questions.explanation: The threshold is 0.5 mL/kg/h x 80 kg x 6 h = 240 mL. Producing less than this over 6 hours meets the urine output criterion for AKI.

questions.stem: Classify the causes of AKI as prerenal, intrinsic and postrenal, giving two examples of each, and explain how urine sodium and osmolality help to separate prerenal AKI from acute tubular necrosis.
markingGuide: Prerenal: reduced perfusion, examples hypovolaemia, heart failure, sepsis, haemorrhage, NSAIDs/ACE inhibitors
Intrinsic: damage to nephron, examples ATN, glomerulonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis
Postrenal: obstruction, examples prostatic enlargement, bilateral stones, tumour
Prerenal: healthy tubules reabsorb sodium and water so low urine sodium and concentrated urine
ATN: damaged tubules cannot reabsorb so high urine sodium and urine osmolality near that of plasma
questions.explanation: Classification by site directs treatment: restore perfusion, treat the intrinsic disease, or relieve obstruction. Urinary indices reflect whether the tubules are still functioning.

questions.stem: Describe how CKD is defined and staged. Explain why both eGFR and albuminuria are used and how a patient with eGFR 55 and ACR 40 mg/mmol would be categorised.
markingGuide: Definition: abnormal structure or function persisting for more than 3 months
GFR categories G1 (90 or more), G2 (60-89), G3a (45-59), G3b (30-44), G4 (15-29), G5 (below 15)
Albuminuria categories A1 (ACR below 3), A2 (3-30), A3 (above 30 mg/mmol)
Both predict progression and cardiovascular risk; albuminuria marks glomerular damage independent of GFR
eGFR 55 is G3a and ACR 40 is A3, so G3a A3
questions.explanation: GFR measures remaining filtering capacity while albuminuria indicates glomerular injury, and the combination predicts risk better than either alone. The patient in this question is G3a A3.

questions.stem: Explain the mechanisms of the main metabolic complications of advanced renal failure: hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, anaemia and CKD-mineral and bone disorder.
markingGuide: Hyperkalaemia: reduced potassium excretion as functioning nephrons are lost
Metabolic acidosis: reduced hydrogen ion excretion and ammonia generation
Anaemia: reduced erythropoietin production, normocytic normochromic
Reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation gives low calcitriol, hypocalcaemia
Secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease
questions.explanation: Each complication corresponds to a lost kidney function: excretion of potassium and acid, production of erythropoietin, and activation of vitamin D. Understanding the mechanisms explains the treatments, such as dietary restriction, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and vitamin D analogues.
